main.summary: Xiahou Xuan defends the Warring States general Yue Yi. People blamed him for not storming the cities of Ju and Jimo in time; the author argues that Yue Yi aimed to win the world by humaneness and rightness, not by a quick, bloody victory, and so deliberately took the two cities slowly in order to keep to what is right. It was not a mistake.
main.translation:
Most people now judge Yue Yi poorly because he did not take Ju and Jimo in time, so I set out the matter and discuss it.

In seeking the meaning of the worthies of old, one should put the great and the far first; only if the road is roundabout and cannot be made to go through is it right to stop. Now, perhaps the aim of Master Yue has not been fully grasped? And because many think poorly of him, the worthy of former times loses his meaning for the future. Is that not a pity! Look at the letter Yue Yi left for King Hui of Yan: he seems very nearly to have known the springs of events and to have accorded with the Way, acting by ritual propriety from beginning to end. Again, he explained to King Zhao: "Yi Yin banished Taijia without doubt, and Taijia accepted banishment without resentment; this is to hold a great enterprise in perfect impartiality and keep the world in one's heart." One who wishes to carry the measure of the Way and virtue to its utmost, and strives to keep the world in his heart, must bring his lord to flourishing and match his aims to those of the former kings. If lord and minister tally, the great enterprise is settled. At that time, Master Yue's purpose met a chance that comes once in a thousand years. An age with a chance once in a thousand years must also carry out a Way that flourishes once in a thousand years; how could he be confined to the traces of the moment and stop at mere annexation?

Annexation was not what Master Yue deigned to do; strengthening Yan while abandoning the Way was not what he sought either. Not stooping to petty gain, with no thought for what is close at hand, not seeking small success: this is the mind that takes in the whole world. So the raising of the matter of Qi was the way to set his lever in motion and move the four seas. To attack Qi in order to make clear the righteousness of the King of Yan: this was an army not raised for profit. To besiege the cities without bringing harm to the common people: this made his humane heart plain far and near. The whole country did not scheme for its own credit, and he removed the cruel without relying on force: this was perfect virtue complete under Heaven. Taking this whole virtue to lead the states, he came near to the deeds of Tang and Wu.

Master Yue meant to spread the great principle and so let the two cities go, to shepherd the people with clear good faith and wait for Qi to wear itself out. He meant to make the people of Jimo and Ju turn to hate their own ruler and wish to lay down their arms and rely on us; even if their defenders were still loyal and good at holding the line, their cleverness would have nowhere to be used. Then "seeking humaneness and finding it" was the rightness of the Grand Officer of Jimo; "when in office and at one's wits' end, move on" was the way of Weizi going to Zhou. He opened a road ever wider to wait for the likes of Tian Dan, and let the custom of tolerating the good grow long, so that the will of the knights of Qi could be expressed. The loyal could complete their integrity, the brave could make their rightness plain. It would shine over the Eastern Sea and reach the Chinese lands: my kindness like spring, the people answering like grass, the Way shining through the universe, the wise and clever entrusting their hearts, neighbouring states yearning for him, the four seas craning their necks, wishing to carry the lord of Yan on their heads and gazing up to his fame. The two cities would surely follow, and the royal enterprise would flourish. Though he lingered at two towns, he was hastening towards the world. The misfortune of the change was something the age did not foresee; to be defeated just at the point of completion was the course of fate.

But suppose he had pressed them with force, threatened them with arms, set about assault and capture, and sought a quick credit, making the knights of Yan and Qi shed blood beneath the two cities and flaunting the cruelty of killing and wounding before the people of the four seas. That would be to let loose violence and exchange one disorder for another to achieve his private ends, and the neighbouring states would look on him as on jackals and tigers. He would have greatly cast down the rightness of raising an army and lost the humaneness that rescues the drowning; and he would also have marred the integrity of the knights of Qi, abolished the custom of incorruptness and goodness, covered over a broad and open measure and thrown away the height of kingly virtue. Even if the two cities could nearly have been taken, the deeds of a hegemon-king would have gone far away. Then, even if Yan had annexed Qi, how would it differ from the rulers of the age? How could it overturn the neighbouring states?

Did Master Yue not know how swiftly the two cities could be taken and the matter finished? He saw that once the cities were taken, the great enterprise would be spoilt. Did he not worry that being slow would bring a change? He saw that spoiling the enterprise was the same as a change. Seen in this way, that Yue Yi did not slaughter the two cities cannot be lightly measured.

keyLines.line: 世人多以樂毅不時拔莒、即墨為劣，是以敘而論之
keyLines.en: People mostly judge Yue Yi poorly because he did not take Ju and Jimo in time, so I set out the matter and discuss it
keyLines.note: The opening gives the reason for writing: many criticised Yue Yi for failing to take Ju and Jimo, and the author speaks up for him.

keyLines.line: 伊尹放太甲而不疑，太甲受放而不怨，是存大業於至公而以天下為心者也
keyLines.en: Yi Yin banished Taijia without doubt, and Taijia accepted banishment without resentment; this is to hold a great enterprise in perfect impartiality and keep the world in one's heart
keyLines.note: A quotation from Yue Yi's own letter to King Hui of Yan, praising a ruler and minister who act for the whole world and not for themselves. It is the base on which the author builds his reading of Yue Yi's mind.

keyLines.line: 不屑苟利，心無近事，不求小成，斯意兼天下者也
keyLines.en: Not stooping to petty gain, with no thought for what is close at hand, not seeking small success: this is the mind that takes in the whole world
keyLines.note: Yue Yi aimed at kingly rule and did not chase small gains in front of him; that is what it means to have the world in one's heart.

keyLines.line: 夫討齊以明燕王之義，此兵不興於為利矣
keyLines.en: To attack Qi in order to make clear the righteousness of the King of Yan: this was an army not raised for profit
keyLines.note: Says that the war on Qi was to uphold what is right and not to seek gain.

keyLines.line: 我澤如春，民應如草，道光宇宙，賢智託心
keyLines.en: My kindness is like spring, and the people answer like grass; the Way shines through the universe, and the wise entrust their hearts
keyLines.note: Describes the kingly atmosphere Yue Yi imagined: favour like spring, and the people responding like grass in the wind.

keyLines.line: 樂生豈不知拔二城之速了哉，顧城拔而業乖也
keyLines.en: Did Yue Yi not know how quickly the two cities could be taken? He saw that taking them would spoil the great work
keyLines.note: The core of the essay: Yue Yi knew very well that a hard assault could win quickly; he feared that capturing the cities would work against his larger kingly aim.

keyLines.line: 樂生之不屠二城，未可量也
keyLines.en: That Yue Yi did not slaughter the two cities cannot be lightly measured
keyLines.note: The closing line: Yue Yi's refusal to massacre the two cities shows a depth of purpose which cannot easily be measured.

glossary.en: Yue Yi - a general of Yan
glossary.note: Commander of Yan under King Zhao in the Warring States period. He led an allied army that took more than seventy cities of Qi, leaving only Ju and Jimo.

glossary.en: Ju, Jimo - two cities of Qi
glossary.note: They held out after Yue Yi's attack on Qi, and Jimo later became the base from which Tian Dan won back the state.

glossary.en: Yan Huiwang - King Hui of Yan
glossary.note: Son of King Zhao of Yan. He listened to slander and grew suspicious of Yue Yi, who then fled to Zhao.

glossary.en: Yi Yin fang Taijia - Yi Yin exiled Taijia
glossary.note: In the Shang dynasty (c. 1600-1046 BC), Yi Yin sent the misruling Taijia away to Tonggong and welcomed him back once he had mended his ways. It is told as an act of a loyal minister.
To seize land by force, the opposite of the kingly way.

glossary.en: Tian Dan - a general of Qi
glossary.note: He broke the Yan army with his charge of fire-tailed oxen and won back Qi's land.

glossary.en: qiu ren de ren - 'seeking humaneness and finding it'
glossary.note: From the Analects: those who seek humaneness and gain it have nothing to regret.

glossary.en: Weizi shi Zhou - Weizi went to Zhou
glossary.note: Weizi was an elder half-brother of the tyrant King Zhou of Shang. After Shang fell he turned to the Zhou and was made lord of Song.

main.background: The 'Discourse on Yue Yi' is an essay on history by Xiahou Xuan (courtesy name Taichu) of Wei in the Three Kingdoms period, defending Yue Yi, who was suspected and was said not to have pressed the attack on the two cities. Later, in the Eastern Jin dynasty (317-420), Wang Xizhi copied it in small regular script, and it became one of the most famous small-regular-script models, called the 'summit of small regular script'; later learners often begin from it. Wang Xizhi's original is long lost, and what we see today are later tracings and rubbings. The characters are upright with careful structure, and the brush is restrained and unhurried, which makes it a good first model for the small regular script of the Wei and Jin periods.
